en: The *Āryatārāsragdharāstotra*:
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed Noble Tārā!
She whose beauty is like the rising sun, and who possesses the splendor of the exquisite crest-jewel upon the heads of the gods, which is as red as copper.

O Noble Lady, with devotion I worship your feet— which possess a clearly visible pattern of red lac applied not long ago through contact with prosperity— with my head bowed low by the crown of my cupped hands, and with garlands of fresh flowers of praise offered as a refuge by those who seek deliverance from calamity.
Having fallen into the difficult-to-cross fire of suffering, unfortunate, bewildered, and fleeing in all directions, the fool— distressed by the repeated futility of his efforts—
again hears from others of the splendor of the sun and moon in the sky, like one whose eyes have been pierced.

Bound by hope for the light, I take refuge in you, the destroyer of evil, who leads others to the supreme state. Surely your compassion has operated without distinction throughout the entire path of sentient beings;
therefore, it is certain that even one such as I has been seized within its grasp through that very attachment.
His power is peerless, like the orb of the fierce-rayed sun for the darkness of evil in the entire world;
yet I, though suffering, still burn [with envy]—fie, alas, on my wicked and perverse deed! Fie, fie on me, the unfortunate one, whose darkness is not dispelled even by the light of the sun!

O Blessed One, sole mother of all the world, though you have made yourself our protector, we remain protectorless— poor and parched on the banks of the Haimavatī river, cooled by slabs of ice, within the vast jeweled caves of the city-streets of Ratnadvīpa.
Even the mother cries out many times for the sake of milk and falls into distress; even the father harbors anger toward his son when he is daily intent upon improper desires.
But you are the supreme creeper upon the great wish-fulfilling tree that yields the vast fruit of the aspirations of the three worlds.
To all you grant their desired objects and yet you never undergo any change whatsoever.
O one whose body is ablaze with the fire of the flood of afflictions, sink as you are in the abyss of suffering, make fruitful for me your self-declared vow: "I am the savior of whomever [seeks me]."

"As long as the harsh insults and the surges of suffering for living beings increase until the end, so long does the compassion of those whose minds are held by their vows in the vehicle of the Perfectly Awakened One [increase]. Thus,
with arms raised high, he let out a cry of lamentation under the guise of words of praise.
O Mother, no one else ought to feel such indifference as you do; yet,
seeing others obtain the very prosperity they desired from you,
I burn with an internal fever born of unbearable discontent that increases all the more.
If I am a sinner, why does this great devotion toward You increase within me?

By both Śruti and Smṛti it is said that You alone forcibly remove even sin by Your very name; having cast off the burden of all other activities, how is it that You push [sin] away from me? Tell me the truth, O You whose speech is truth!
"Will the physician, though possessing great compassion, continue to prescribe wholesome food even for one who is dying? Why does he weep?

Thus is he reproached by base individuals such as those characterized by deceit, envy, and pride, both simultaneously and sequentially by their own faults; like a young elephant in a monastery, his shoulders are shared by many.

Because I do not obtain even for a moment the worship of your lotus feet, may this composition of words, humble with the syllables of my wretchedness, be especially fruitful in fulfilling that desire of mine. [Tss 9] Amidst the play of restless waves upon the waters tossed by the winds wandering at the end of an aeon—

O Goddess, from the ocean— where the roar of its tumultuous, splashing waves breaking against the rugged shores resounds like a loud laugh— the shore is now being reached at will by those who, having been overwhelmed by you, have their ships shattered as they sink; they move slowly, motionless, amidst piteous wailing and cries of lamentation.

With their beds resting within houses that were suddenly cleared by the force of a fire—terrifying with its crackling flames and leaping sparks dancing in the lap of the sky as it emerged from the womb of clouds mistaken for smoke;
their crowns bearing hands joined in salutation with palms pressed together; and their commands proclaimed in faltering songs of praise—to you [they belong].
In an instant, they are seized by the enemy elephants, who are as radiant as clouds flashing with rising lightning;
these elephants have fire of hatred generated by the trumpeting of rival tuskers summoned by the humming of swarms of bees clinging to their temples, which are filled with the ichor of rut.

Seated upon the fortress-peak of the summit of his broad crest, his body balanced on the high swing of his tusks' tips, he joyfully defies death by recollecting you amidst the festival of the vine-like tridents formed by the heads of men struck down by the blows of his mature spears.

In the empty wilderness, with eyes fixed upon you with frowning brows and crooked glances, he employs as his servants those bandits whose pride is swollen by the clashing of swords gleaming in their grasped hands;
yet, with the pen of his thought, he unwearyingly and clearly inscribes your name— the very seat of splendor— upon their eyes.
With the frontal globes of intoxicated elephants torn open by the tips of his claws— sharp as the blows of a diamond—
and with the joints of his broad shoulders made vividly gory by being washed in the thick blood flowing from them,
the lion, the enemy of deer, stands nearby, enraged and desiring to pounce, his mouth formidable with its sharp fangs.
Trembling, he turns back and departs, his speech consisting of milk-like meanings from hymns composed by you; yet he is seized by the nooses of Death—
nooses that are the throbbing cords of wide tongues darting from mouths opened wide by the force of the great hissing of serpents, whose forms are distorted by the darkness of swirling smoke.
Having emerged from evil, he becomes intent on enumerating your multitude of virtues; with his soul devoted to you,
he assumes the splendor of ornaments consisting of bracelets of intoxicated bees and garlands of blue water-lilies,
while his hair is pulled by the formidable soldiers of the enemy army, terrified by the knitting of their lord’s brows.

Even one who is abandoned by affectionate kinsmen, whose throat and lips are withered by hunger and thirst, and who is ensnared by the harsh noose of knots in the fierce clamor of a servant full of prattling chatter— he too instantly abandons that miserable calamity if he should go for refuge to the feet of the Noble Tārā. (Tss 16)
They carry weapons that are terrifying due to the grand display of rays, which correspond to the false forms and various costumes created through the sequence of illusory emanations;
yet for one whose misdeeds have been removed by the recollection of the mantras extracted from your Tantra, they become invincible.
The *rakṣas* offered protection with their throats choked by the strings of entrails threaded through the corpses of hungry ghosts;
amidst the darkness of the torrential downpour from the three-fold intoxication of passion, which resembled the form of thundering clouds,
amidst the radiance of weapons flashing like lightning, and amidst the falling rain of arrows.
Though held back at the time of battle by enemies with powerful arm-strength,
that peerless hero— sustained by the vigor you have bestowed— violently crushes the earth of his foes,
[whose blood flows] as a foul-smelling stream of putrid pus trickling from the maces brandished by those arrogant in their evil conduct.
Those whose limbs are bitten and wounded by creatures dwelling within the hollows of the openings of veins clinging to their skin and flesh,
become devoted through the practice of the supreme medicinal pill of service to your feet;
they are born with bodies resembling gold and eyes as broad as lotuses.
He whose ear-vessel has been filled with the traditional teachings offered by his gurus,
yet who, due to a lack of the wealth of learning, falls into silence within assemblies of the wise—
even though he has attained mastery over speech, which is more radiant than all other ornaments— [is truly destitute].

Yet, by the power of devotion to you, he too seizes the lion-thrones of the disputants in the royal assembly. Sleeping on the ground, his body grey with dust and his tattered loincloth hanging open, he crushes the lifespans of lice in a skull-bowl before the bodies of others, seeking to satisfy himself.
Having propitiated you, he resolved to rule the earth— beautiful with the smiles of fly-whisks borne by young maidens,
its dense forests of tusks belonging to elephants blinded by rut, and its sovereignty marked by a single raised parasol;
for he was weary of the various means of service, labor, arts, lack of favor, and the exchange of favors.
Failing to obtain wealth— the fruit of merit accumulated through the store of virtue acquired in previous births— those who are destitute, by entreating you, O Mother of the wretched, for their sake,
obtain from the earth treasures of gold that have been extinguished by fate.
Dejected at the loss of his livelihood, being rebuked by his wife whose garment was torn,
and abandoned from afar by his own kin, children, friends, and relatives because of his self-centeredness—
he shall report his own suffering to you regarding houses whose boundaries have been dug up by the tips of horses' hooves.

He rules over a city where sleep is awakened by the jingling of bracelets from the women within his inner apartments; he possesses a discus that kisses the quarters of the sky, a woman adorned with auspicious marks and shimmering rays,
a preeminent elephant with six tusks, and a noble horse with hair as dark and beautiful as a peacock’s throat.

By a mere fragment of a portion of your grace, O Blessed One, one becomes a radiant jewel with brilliant rays, possessing stainless qualities and a full treasury; one becomes a commander-in-chief with heroic troops,
and a sovereign whose delightful trysting-place is provided by moonstones fragrant with the water of sandalwood.
Out of passion for sporting with his beloved, performing sincere hospitality with offerings newly prepared,
and having attained supernatural powers through your science, the Lord of the Vidyādharas goes to the honeyed grove of Mount Malaya,
his thick and lofty club-like arms darkened by the luster of his sword and his bracelets shimmering.
Their breasts were embraced by pearl necklaces; their long eyes rivaled the blue water-lilies at their ears;
the unrestrained bees were intoxicated by the abundant fragrance of the fresh jasmine in their noble braids;
and the drums of their magnificent anklets resounded loudly, accompanied by the continuous tinkling of their girdles.
The daughters of the gods, joyful with the intoxication of love, respectfully pray for you as their protector—
[you who dwell] amidst golden lotus-pools covered with jewels, possessing garlands of diamond filaments,
and beneath a canopy of pollen stirred up by the sweet honey of the emerging Pārijāta trees.
Having performed your worship with the sweetness of musical instruments provided by the celestial nymphs of the city of Amarāvatī, who are skilled in playing the lute and flute,
he enjoys for a long time an excursion to the Nandana grove in waters fragrant with camphor,
cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, agallochum, nalada, and kakkola.

Those whose inner hearts are transformed by devotion to you sport with beautiful women in the Mandākinī river— a stream of water with slow-moving ripples resting in the whirlpools of their deep bosoms, which have subdued the fierce pride of Kāmadeva— by means of playing in its waters of abundant splendor, through the power of the intense merit they have ripened.
His commands were saluted by the leaders of the host of gods, whose heads bowed under the weight of humility;
he was seated upon the lap of heaven, mounted on a celestial elephant whose limbs were resplendent with tinkling ornaments;
and his body was covered with a profuse horripilation as it was gently encircled by the creeper-like arms of Śacī.
Purified by the falling glances of your eyes, Hīra protects the divine earth with his forearm unscarred.
He is the canopy for the celestial splendor of the Sugata seated upon the crest-jewel ornament,
filling the three worlds with rays more brilliant than ten million rising young suns.

Your form— with one foot firmly planted in the *ālīḍha* stance, while Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and Viṣṇu bow down under the weight of its successive steps— is meditated upon by those born into this world for the destruction of the fear of *saṃsāra*.
Some behold it as wrathful, with the mass of its staff-like arms raised aloft, weapons flashing from their rays.

It is fierce with the tumultuous clamor of a great sport of intoxication— the wild beating of cymbals by Vetālas at the shore, their frantic dancing accompanied by a terrifying laughter that strikes fear into enemies, and the formidable display of the hoods of the serpent encircling the expanse of the sky as its natural ornament.
Some, however, [saw] within each single pore of his body the entire expanse of the sky and the surface of the earth,
filled with Brahmās, Indras, Rudras, and others— humans, gods, siddhas, gandharvas, and nāgas—
remaining in their own abodes; and they saw hundreds of infinite Sugatas, variegated by their emanations, stationed in places that pervade the circle of all directions.
Some [behold him] as a wondrous being, worshipped by the three worlds, whose essential nature consists of all states—both moving and stationary;
others [behold him] as having the crimson redness of the sun with rays more intensely reddened than lac-dye or vermilion;
and still others [behold him] as blue-black like the crushed powder of a magnificent, dense sapphire.

Some perceive Your universal form as whiter than the milk churned from the Ocean of Milk, others as golden-hued; it appears like crystal, differentiated by the application of various adjuncts. You are the sole witness of the reality of all objects of knowledge, revealed by the lamp of omniscient wisdom.
Either the Omniscient One himself or his son knows directly the enumeration of your multitude of virtues;
as for the fact that one like me, having opened my mouth, utters the cawing of a crow,
that failure is a cause for laughter to the mind afflicted by the pain born of the fever of intense suffering.
That which I am about to request first of all you, as my superior knower, will be a cause for the satisfaction of the hearts of the ignorant through the extraordinary effort of your speech; yet,
it is like poison to a loving kinsman, for I must utter words of sorrow before you.
Even for one who knows the truth, there is suffering; yet, through the lightness of heart, one finds as it were a state of well-being.
O you who are like the visible crescent moon in the ocean of the bliss of virtue, bestow your cooling gaze;
O you of profound compassion, grant nourishment through instructions in knowledge and destroy the darkness within.

In me, whose mind has been purified by the waters of your hymn of praise, I have perceived a single source of ultimate welfare; for among all beings in this world, the mere chanting of your qualities is unfailing.
Whatever merit I have obtained by praising the multitude of your qualities, even though their parts are beyond measure and limit—
By that merit, which is like the tasting of the sweet flavor of the fruit of one’s desire for an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and which is to be enjoyed until liberation,

may this world immediately proceed to that land called Sukhāvatī— the earth of the sons of the Sugata, marked with the auspicious *svastika* sign upon the soles of the feet of the noble Lord of the World (*Ārya-Lokeśvara*).
